content: Blood is the preferred specimen for HIV testing because it contains a higher concentration of HIV antibodies compared to oral fluid. Additionally, blood allows for further testing, such as determining viral load, recent infection status, HIV type and subtype, drug resistance, as well as testing for syphilis and hepatitis. Blood can be collected via fingerstick or venipuncture. However, participants are often reluctant to undergo multiple blood draws or finger pricks due to discomfort and concerns about confidentiality, as repeated pricking may suggest the need for additional testing in infected individuals. A single fingerstick typically yields about 200 μL of blood or less, though some systems can collect up to 500 μL. Venous blood collection using evacuated (vacuum) tubes is more efficient, as it can collect larger volumes (5–10 mL or more), enabling multiple tests to be performed. Collecting extra blood is advantageous for quality control, repeat testing, or storing specimens for future testing. Evacuated tubes containing the anticoagulant EDTA are particularly useful as they provide both cellular and plasma fractions. If serum is required, untreated tubes should be used. Plasma or serum aliquots should be prepared shortly after collection, refrigerated, transported, and frozen at a central laboratory. Alternatively, they can be frozen on-site and transported on freezer packs to the central laboratory without thawing. Repeated freezing and thawing should be avoided to maintain specimen quality. Blood collected for CD4+ T-cell counting must be stored at ambient temperature, and specialized long-life blood tubes can stabilize CD4+ T-cells for up to seven days, easing transportation and testing requirements. Dried blood spots (DBS) are easy to prepare and serve as backup specimens if plasma samples are lost or spoiled. However, DBS is not ideal for HIV serology using enzyme immunoassays (EIA) due to high background optical density readings. Some EIA kits have protocols for DBS, but these often require optimization. For HIV testing in challenging survey environments, participants with reactive tests are counseled to seek confirmatory testing elsewhere. Investigators may use preliminary results for data analysis without waiting for confirmatory test outcomes. Oral fluid specimens can be stored at 4°C to 37°C for up to 21 days, with freezing required for extended storage. Once thawed, oral fluid specimens can only be refrozen once more. Urine is the CDC-recommended specimen for nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) to detect Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in men. First-catch urine specimens contain bacteria similar to those in urethral swabs, making urine a suitable alternative when swabs are undesirable, such as in population-based studies or when multiple samples are needed. For women, vaginal swabs are the optimal specimen for detecting Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae due to their higher sensitivity compared to urine. Self-collected vaginal swabs are as sensitive and specific as clinician-collected swabs and may be more acceptable to some women, reducing staffing requirements. Vaginal swabs do not replace cervical exams for diagnosing other urogenital infections. Rectal swabs are recommended for men who have sex with men (MSM) for NAAT detection of Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. These can also be collected from female sex workers (FSW) and may be self-collected or clinician-collected. Oropharyngeal swabs are used for detecting Neisseria gonorrhoeae via NAAT, though false positives may occur due to non-harmful Neisseria species in the oropharynx. Urethral swabs, historically used for STI diagnosis in men, are now less favored due to discomfort and the availability of urine-based NAATs, which are CDC-recommended for diagnosing Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Specimen handling, storage, and transport vary by type. For example, DBS specimens should be dried thoroughly at room temperature before refrigeration or freezing. Blood collected in anticoagulant tubes must be centrifuged, and plasma should be frozen within 24 hours for molecular testing. Proper labeling and tracking of specimens are essential for linking biological and survey data. Specimens may be temporarily stored in refrigerators or cooler boxes with cold packs, depending on assay requirements. Long-term storage requires informed consent from participants, specifying storage duration and control over specimen use. This includes documentation, standard operating procedures (SOPs), external quality assessments, and quality-control retesting. Proficiency testing involves blinded sample panels sent to testing sites to evaluate accuracy, with corrective actions taken for poor performance.
